LNG must be stored as a cryogenic liquid at approximately −162°C (111 K). Most LNG is exported, and there is currently limited use as a transportation fuel. U.S. LNG capacity is expanding, and significant growth is anticipated for regasification and carrier fleet infrastructure to move LNG through the supply chain. Delivered prices to airports for LNG currently compete with jet fuel on an energy basis; however, fuel handling, storage, and safety costs related to cryogenic fuel in the aviation context need to be considered. There are no known estimates for addition costs for fuel handling, storage, and dispensing for LNG as an aviation fuel. However, there is extensive use of natural gas (in gaseous form) in the U.S., including for generating electricity and space heating, and a large pipeline infrastructure exists for these purposes (EIA 2024c). This existing infrastructure could likely be leveraged with additional liquefaction facilities added to support aviation use. LE was also evaluated for potential aviation use. U.S. ethane production is dominated by petrochemical demand, with approximately 80% used to produce ethylene. LE production and transport is energy intensive involving extraction, cooling, liquefaction, and handling. LE is mainly used as a feedstock in the production of ethylene. Ethane is normally separated from natural gas or hydrocarbon liquids and liquefied at approximately −89°C (184 K) to reduce its volume for economical transport via ships or rail. Considerable volumes of LE are exported, leaving limited availability for alternative uses like aviation fuel. Production has been steadily increasing and is forecast to continue growing, supported by expanding natural gas liquids production and new cracking facilities (EIA 2021). Both existing and planned ethane infrastructure, including pipelines, fractionators, storage, and export terminals, are designed to serve petrochemical demand and would require significant investment to retrofit for aviation. Prices of ethane at U.S. hubs like Mont Belvieu, Texas, remain very low and stable, considerably cheaper compared with Jet A (EIA 2025b, 2024a). Jet X is in early-stage research, and it is anticipated that these fuels would have no or low aromatics, which reduces soot formation. ASTM’s non-drop-in jet fuel group is exploring alternative chemistries. Research is in early stages to identify fuel properties and biogenic aromatics. Once Jet X fuel properties are defined, extensive materials, equipment, and engine/turbine research and testing will be required to determine the ability to use existing infrastructure and/or identify upgrades necessary to enable the fuel. Another critical safety aspect is segregating Jet A/SAF at an airport from an alternate liquid aviation fuel to avoid contamination.
